summary: FTP, as defined in RFC 959, cannot tell apart several DNS names registered to one IP address. This document defines a new FTP command, HOST, that lets clients and servers identify individual virtual hosts.

plainLanguage.summary: One building can have many shops. This adds a way for a visitor to say which shop they want when they walk in.

questions: what is the ftp host command
how do ftp virtual hosts work
subtitle: A new FTP command that lets a client say which virtual host it wants when many names share one IP address.

tldr.problem: An FTP server tells connections apart by IP address, so every DNS name on the same address gets the same file system and the same authentication.
tldr.mechanism: The client sends HOST with a hostname before logging in, so the server can pick the right virtual host, much as the Host header does in HTTP/1.1.
tldr.outcome: Different virtual hosts can offer different file systems and authentication on one address. The RFC updates RFC 959 and the command is registered with IANA.

today: RFC 7151 is a Proposed Standard published in March 2014 that updates RFC 959. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why FTP Needs a HOST Command
sections.content:
Many DNS names often resolve to a single IP address, which creates a virtual host: a host that appears independent but shares resources with others. An FTP server tells incoming connections apart by IP address, not by DNS name. So all names sharing an address land on the same server and share the same Network Virtual File System (NVFS).

Virtual hosts therefore cannot offer different file systems or different authentication systems. Typical clients resolve the hostname to an address and then ignore the name for the rest of the session, so fixing this needs changes to both the user protocol interpreter (user-PI) and the server protocol interpreter (server-PI).

The RFC points out that HTTP/1.0 had the same problem and HTTP/1.1 solved it with the Host header field. The goal here is similar parity for FTP. This document updates RFC 959.
sections.plainLanguage: If a hundred shops share one street number, the mail carrier cannot tell them apart. The HOST command adds the shop name to the address.

sections.title: HOST Command Syntax
sections.content:
The command is HOST SP hostname CRLF, and the success reply is a 220 reply. The hostname is either a domain or an IP literal. The command word is case independent, and domain names are case insensitive.

The hostname SHOULD be the name used to find the server's IP address, after turning any short alias into a fully qualified name but before resolving a CNAME to its canonical name. Internationalized names are supported only as IDNA A-labels, for example HOST xn--e1afmkfd.com.

A client given an IPv4 or IPv6 literal MAY send it, with IPv6 in square brackets, such as HOST [2001:db8::c000:201]. If the literal does not match the server's own address, the server MUST answer 504. The client MUST NOT send a port number, and the server MUST answer 501 if it does, because the connection is already made.
sections.plainLanguage: You write the shop's name on the slip, not the door number. You also do not need to write how you got there, since you are already standing at the door.

sections.title: Semantics and Login Order
sections.content:
If a HOST command is sent, it MUST be issued before the user is authenticated, so that the authentication scheme and set of authorized users can depend on the chosen host. A user-PI MUST send it after opening the connection, or after any REIN command, and before USER.

If HOST is sent more than once before authentication, the server MUST act as if only the last one was sent. If it is sent after authentication, the server MUST treat it as an erroneous command sequence and return 503. The effect of HOST MUST be reset by REIN, and a new HOST MUST follow it.

On receiving HOST, the server SHOULD check the name is a valid virtual host and set up the matching environment. What that involves is not specified. The response to HOST is a sensible time for the server to send a personalized welcome message. HOST also combines with ACCT, with AUTH and ADAT from RFC 2228 and RFC 4217, and with the TLS "server_name" extension, in which case the server MUST check that the HOST name matches it.
sections.plainLanguage: You must say which shop you want before you show your ticket. If you say the wrong one, you can correct yourself, but only until you have been let in.

sections.title: Errors and FEAT
sections.content:
Servers that do not know HOST SHOULD reply 500 or 502. A client getting one of these SHOULD assume the server does not do virtual servers this way, and MAY log in as if HOST had not been sent. A 501 SHOULD be sent for a syntactically invalid hostname, and a 504 SHOULD be sent when a valid-looking name is not a virtual host here. A temporarily unavailable host gets a 421 and the connection is closed. After 501 or 504, the server MUST either ignore the HOST command or close the connection. Any other error reply means the client SHOULD assume the virtual host is unavailable and stop.

A server that gets USER without any HOST SHOULD NOT reject it, since older clients never send HOST. It MAY use a default virtual host or a combined environment.

A server supporting HOST MUST list the single word HOST in its reply to FEAT, SHOULD in upper case, as one line of the multi-line 211 response.
sections.plainLanguage: If the front desk has never heard of the shop-name slip, you can just walk in the old way. If it knows the slip but not your shop, it says no and lets you try again.

sections.title: Security and TLS Interaction
sections.content:
When a second HOST arrives before authentication, the server MUST reset the authentication environment. That keeps each virtual host's security environment separate, so one host can use one user and password list and another a different one.

When HOST is used with the FTP security extensions, the client SHOULD check that the hostname it gave matches the identity in the server's X.509 certificate, to prevent man-in-the-middle attacks. The HOST command SHOULD come before the security handshake, unless the client provides "server_name" in the extended client hello (RFC 6066). Otherwise the server may pick the wrong virtual host and present the wrong certificate, and the client cannot verify the server. If the client does send "server_name", it MAY send HOST after the handshake, but the server MUST verify the two names match.

Clients SHOULD protect credentials with the FTP security extensions; general FTP security issues are in RFC 2577.
sections.plainLanguage: Tell the front desk which shop you want before you hand over your ID, or you might show your ID to the wrong shop.

sections.title: Alternatives That Did Not Work
sections.content:
Appendix A explains why other ideas were judged unworkable.

  • Overloading CWD. CWD works only after login, so all virtual hosts would share one authentication scheme, and a user could easily move to other virtual hosts.
  • Overloading ACCT. ACCT comes after USER and PASS, so there is no way to be sure the certificate matches the right virtual host before credentials are sent.
  • Overloading USER as foo@example.com. The syntax is ambiguous with network credentials that already use username@hostname, and it has the same certificate problem.

The conclusion is that supporting virtual hosts needs both client and server changes, so a new command is the most likely solution.
sections.plainLanguage: People tried hiding the shop name inside other forms, but those forms are only handed over after you have already gone in or shown your ID. A new slip fixes it.
